text: We are quite fortunate that we had corporates who have come forward to support us over the years, given MENDAKI's focus, especially on education.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Particularly starting with scholarships and bursaries because that is, I think; while I would say lowest hanging fruit, but I think it is quite core to much of the work that we do.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we have had SIA over the years; we have had GIC; Micron; MiRXES and others, who have come forward and given us.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But it is really about also the community coming forward because it is not just about scholarships and bursaries, but if you look at the contribution that I have shared in my speech, such as Micron providing opportunities, or internship opportunities, for many of our young students who have perhaps never seen the insides of a semiconductor and would never have considered careers in that space.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Sharael Taha has shared how some of the youths were taken to Rolls Royce and others, so that they can look into growth industries and some also visited the Airshow recently to have a look at some of the defence technologies that are available.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we are using various platforms and opportunities to open minds, open conversations with many of our youths who may come from low-income families especially, who may not have had the exposures, but now given the chance to be exposed, to have internship opportunities, to be mentored.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As I shared, MSD Pharma, for example, with their data scientists, AI specialists, cybersecurity specialists to give them opportunities and mix around with professionals who they may never have met through regular channels.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think this is one way in which we want to build social capital.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, yes, we have started with certain corporates but I would not underestimate the impact and effect.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We hope that more will come forward, especially through the professional network.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We hope that this brings about building up social capital within the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to encourage more to contribute back in small ways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It does not have to be big corporates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have members from the Indian/Muslim community as well, who came forward to set up funds because some Indian/Muslims did not qualify for TTFS, for example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But there are efforts on the ground that came ground-up because they want to do something for the community, including those who have qualified for certain schemes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we are providing a wide range of opportunities but I think it is more than just scholarships and bursaries; but providing opportunities, providing social capital, providing mentorship.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Just some clarifications in Malay, Mr Chairman. :   My thanks to Senior Minister of State Zaqy for sharing that the MTS has been expanded further to include subjects, like Additional Maths, as well as Biology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: My second question: can we also provide specific programmes to encourage learning of skills in subjects, like AI and cybersecurity, so that our students and workers will have the best chance to work in the growth industries?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In Malay):   I thank Mr Sharael Taha for the good question.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If we look at our MTS programme, we do have a fairly packed curriculum, where we see our children spending three to four hours each week in our MTS centres.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In these sessions, as we can see from the curriculum, they are required to take two subjects today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some of them attend virtual classes after their in-person sessions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we also need to give priority to their schooling and their tuition sessions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, I also recognise that among the programmes that we want them to attend, as I have mentioned to Mr Saktiandi Supaat, we also want them to be given the opportunity to have internships, join learning journeys, and at times, during the Raikan Ilmu month for example, we give them the flexibility to enjoy learning journey opportunities outside, as what has been done under FA3 with Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want our youths to be given the opportunity to be mentored as well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Here, some of them are given the opportunity under the #amPowered programme, as well as the mentoring programme under Ms Rahayu Mahzam within FA3, to share experiences with our professionals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We aim to provide these opportunities beyond our MTS youths, by extending this network to other youths in our M3 towns.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We hope to use all the resources in our M3 towns, so that we can reach out to more youths who can benefit from the programmes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope Mr Sharael Taha will continue to give his support, and this goes for other Members here too, so that we can provide better opportunities for our students.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and then, Ms Nadia Samdin.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I have a question on wakaf for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In some of these cases, you may find it challenging to find the beneficiaries and locate the rightful heirs to the wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And when you have a fixed asset, the returns from fixed assets are not very high.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition to that, the beneficiaries that were named some time 100 or some 200 years ago, either the country does not exist anymore; the village does not exist anymore; let alone the person does not exist anymore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is not just faced by communities like ourselves, it is faced all over the world.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the meantime, there are good discussions, conferences to evolve the concept of wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the last fatwa conference, I had a good discussion with Dr Sano, for example, who said that today, the instruments of wakaf has evolved.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, there is something called a temporary wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That means you pledge your Corpus Fund for, say, one year and that you cannot use it; but the returns will then go into the wakaf – the Corpus Fund goes back to you after that one-year contract.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, that is an evolving and a new way of doing wakaf and whether or not we can do something about the previous and older wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think for now let us keep to the trust that has been put to our generation, to try as best as we can to execute the will or the intention of those before us who put this wakaf in our trust to benefit the people they wanted to.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And I do not believe this is the last time we will be doing it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I said just now that we will have to move on to do important things that we need to do for the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I foresee that we will probably need to raise funds again because it does not look like this conflict will be resolved fairly quickly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On the second question, all of us need to recognise two things about Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We may have a strong government, a strong country, but we are a small country.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, when we go out and say things, our foreign policy is based on our long-term interests as a small country.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, it is to safeguard our Independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, security, and all for the sake of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And these things are most important, in fact, more important for a small country than a big country.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, when we say things, I hope people understand the context upon which we say it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, our position on Israel has been consistent.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have said that from the start, Israel has a legitimate right to defend itself from acts of terror.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, every country has a right of defence against acts of terror.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the case of Israel, it was the incident on 7 October.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And I hope, as leaders, we try to educate people who talk about this to understand the context, what the Government said and why the Government said it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think it is important that we live as Singaporeans to know why these things have to be said the way they are.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And that is, again, a consistent departure from just calling the right for self-defence with the need to balance it with the right of human dignity and human rights, too.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are diverse and if our solution to a small country is to be strong, our solution in being diverse is to be united.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And that is why, even as a Minister, I may have my sentiments about the Palestinians, fellow Muslims, but I must also, as a Muslim leader and a Minister in Cabinet in a multiracial, multi-religious society country like ours, speak with one voice in Cabinet inasmuch as Singaporeans should be united and speak with one voice because we need to protect Singapore's national interests both domestically and internationally.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A united people, a united Government, that is how we become a strong government, a strong country, despite being small.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But I recognise that Singapore Muslims do have connections with the Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we also should recognise that we are in a unique position and often not the same situation as many other Muslim communities, especially when they are in the majority.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And, therefore, for us being diverse, we have to work together to preserve the peace between ourselves, never be driven, never be divided, and, as I have shared in the Committee of Supply debate, our community thus far has shown and proven themselves where citizenry is concerned.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And I hope that as the situation unravels over the next few months, we continue to hold this, that we must never be divided, we must always seek to unite because we are diverse.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And that is the only way Singapore can survive.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There being no further clarifications, let us move on with the debate.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to start by sharing with this House a recent experience I had.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In late January this year, I was at our National Stadium to watch the Coldplay concert.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Sometime during the show, the lead singer, Chris Martin, said something along the following lines; maybe not exactly in those words, but something along the following lines.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: He said, "Tonight is a special night in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We have so many fans from different countries with different religions, all coming together to watch a concert in Singapore happily, peacefully and safely." After he said this, the Australian guy next to me instantaneously shouted, "Lee Kuan Yew".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And yes, Mr Chairman, this is the multiracial, multicultural and multi-religious Singapore that Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his team has created for us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And I am very confident this is also the Singapore that our People's Action Party (PAP) Government will continue to build for many more generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Besides Taylor Swift, who is currently in Singapore, there have been many popular concerts last year and this year by international and regional renowned performers, such as Black Pink, Coldplay and Ed Sheeran.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And I am also reliably informed that Taylor Swift is currently the most popular solo artist in the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I do not know of any other city in the world that has managed to host such most popular world-class events within two months of each other.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: For this, we must recognise and compliment MCCY and its many partners for having the ability, capacity and mobility to seize opportunities that come our way.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Apart from concerts, the Sports Hub also hosted several major international and regional sporting events, and more than 140 National School games and School Sport events.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Singaporeans can also now use many facilities at the Sports Hub which are open to the public.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: This has made the Sports Hub more accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Importantly, hosting these major events make significant contributions to the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: They give a big boost to our tourism sector, especially in areas, such as hospitality, retail, travel and dining.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Therefore, as a natural consequence, with so many more world-class major events in Singapore, I think it would also mean that more 9% GST will be collected from our tourists and this would ultimately translate to more goodies and more infrastructure and more good news for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And why has Singapore been able to host such major events successfully?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Some commentators point to the possible grants given in return for exclusivity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I think it is much more than that.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Singapore projects as an attractive entertainment and sports events hub because we have a strategic location, quality infrastructure, safety, efficiency and diverse cultural offerings that allow us to present a complete package in pitches to host such major events.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Maybe, just maybe, a new equally exciting indoor venue could be built to replace the Indoor Stadium.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: At the same time, whilst many Singaporeans and tourists can enjoy the many spectacular events in Singapore, I think we can also do more by providing cheaper or maybe free tickets to our lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As an example, whenever the Suzuki Cup matches are played in Singapore, I would get a sponsor to purchase bulk tickets and these are distributed to our lower-income families in Potong Pasir.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Our residents go as a family and they enjoyed the football matches.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Mr Chairman, I focus my cut on the value that sports and youths can bring to building community, promote inclusivity and strengthen social cohesion.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The value of sports is beyond the physical.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Its value is multifaceted, encompassing also psychological, social and economic benefits, with its significance observed at all levels of society, too: at the individual, community and globally.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Beyond the obvious benefits of health and exercise, sports has the power to strengthen well-being, unity in diversity and organic cultural exchange in communities.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Importantly, sports has the power to galvanise and rally.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: We were in awe of her success and achievements in 2023, and taken to her example in terms of her determination, resilience and ability to overcome adversity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: When Joseph Schooling won the Olympic Gold in the 100-metre Butterfly in 2016, the sentiment of national pride was much the same.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Few things rally people, community and a nation more than a celebration of a fellow countryman's great success in sports.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The barrier to entry to sporting success is relatively low in that it does not matter whether one is a populous country or a country with wide and sizeable geographical areas.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: I urge the Ministry to look closely and more strongly at sports as a means to rally and bring people closer together.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Those of us who have engaged in sports and continue to do so will agree that it builds character, values and a certain resilience that cannot be replicated in the classroom.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Team sports further engender a spirit of responsibility, trust in others, camaraderie and a sense of team like no other.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: There are three things that I hope the Ministry will focus on as part of this Budget, as far as sports is concerned.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Our athletes need our support to do well, for they spend a good portion of their hours, days and weeks, even years on end to achieve the success for the country.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: In fact, for a good portion of the time where their peers spend building careers and income, the prime of the young lives of these athletes are consumed in honing their sport, optimising their performance and pushing their physical bodies for peak outcomes, for which, sometimes, injuries can occur.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Where there is talent in our Singaporeans and they are willing to go far with us in terms of their sporting excellence, I propose we spare no effort for them to give their best for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: While we already have examples of success in individual sportsmen and sportswomen, we need to do better for team sports as well.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: It does take much more deliberate investment, a sustained care in the planning over years if not decades for the sport, and a wider systemic approach to develop young talent within a team sport.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: However, the benefit of being able to see a multiplicity of individuals in team sports, where we have a broad representation of athletes from all communities playing together for the national team, is emblematic of the kind of Singapore we hope to build.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: It resonates at a deeper level for us as a people and it becomes a palpable vision of the society we want for ourselves.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Third, I hope for the Ministry to narrate the value of Sports better for the ordinary Singaporean and help make it easy for people to participate in them en masse.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: The benefit of sports in health and mental well-being cannot be understated and should continue to be emphasised at the level of the individual.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: However, the societal benefit of sport can only be realised if everyone participates, enjoys and interacts with one another in play and activity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Even for relatively individual sports, it is possible, with some creativity, to encourage togetherness and cohesion in the activity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: For example, even for the solitary activity of running, which some may prefer, there are running clubs where people may build friendships, find commonality and meet others through their collective joy and passion in the specific sport.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Such cohesion and strong relationships make for a sustained participation in sports and more opportunity to bring people together.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: My other area of emphasis in this cut is for the Ministry to continue harnessing the potential of our youths.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: In fact, we saw quite a relatively young audience earlier on from St Joseph's Institution and we talked about our ageing population often and, indeed, this is an important concern.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: However, by a similar proportion, it also means that the number of youths are in relative decline and youths are a much valued resource.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: I believe we can do better to engage our youths, harness their creativity and innovation, as well as curate ideas through their perspectives and share their willingness to challenge conventional wisdom and current solutions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: This is an important aspect of our nation-building exercise and as the Government moves ahead in its plans for Forward SG.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Chairman, amidst the emergence of new and lesser-known sports disciplines where Singaporean athletes have excelled on the international stage, it becomes imperative to explore avenues for providing support and recognition to athletes in these niche sports.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: As sports, such as tchoukball and powerlifting, gain prominence, albeit not featured in major games, such as the Southeast Asian (SEA) Games, there arises a critical need to empower aspiring athletes in these disciplines.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: How does the Ministry intend to provide support to athletes of emerging sports, ensuring equitable opportunities for sharing excellence across all disciplines?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How can we show that we have not forgotten the contributions and personal sacrifices of those who have brought us such exhilaration and joy, as well as shared anguish, competing against the best in the region and, indeed, the world?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I will touch on two points: (a) helping retired athletes to transit to a work career; and (b) providing healthcare support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is MCCY's assessment of the scheme thus far?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had highlighted that much more is now known about the health conditions associated with sports, not just the usual knee and strain injuries we are familiar with, but also brain injuries caused by certain contact sports.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As these conditions will remain with our retired athletes for the duration of their lives, I had called for some additional help for them to foot such healthcare bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had suggested that a task force be formed to look into the feasibility of this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, to echo the point made earlier by my colleague Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman, we have seen the rise of emerging sports in Singapore where our athletes are performing well internationally in sports, such as tchoukball and powerlifting.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While tchoukball is not a major sport globally, Singapore has been proactive in promoting and supporting it alongside other sports.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This continues the excellent work of athletes that are still flying our Singapore flag high and should be supported in some way by donors, supporters and the Government.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that Singapore has a strong sports development system to support athletes across a variety of sports.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's sports associations and federations often provide funding, training facilities, coaching and administrative support for athletes competing in their respective sports.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has national sports institutes looking into athlete development and training as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, we provide funding and support for sports development through organisations like Sport Singapore, and this funding may be allocated to national sports associations, sports clubs and athletes to help cover training expenses, travel costs for competitions and other related expenses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are aware of these initiatives to support mainstream sports and may they long continue, can MCCY share what it is doing to support aspiring athletes in emerging sports to pursue their dream of sporting excellence?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This was the focus of my speech during a Motion on sporting excellence which I filed in July 2023 alongside my colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: From July 2023 until now, our national football team has won matches against Guam twice as well as Taiwan once and were defeated by Tajikistan, South Korea and Thailand respectively.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: We have also appointed a new coach, Tsutomu Ogura, who will replace his countryman who was sacked after a string of disappointing results.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In 2017, my colleague Mr Pritam Singh had asked a Parliamentary Question about how the Government exercised oversight over how monies are used by the NSAs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I would also like to know what is the framework for determining how much funding each NSA gets and what benchmarks are put in place to determine whether an NSA is performing its function in a satisfactory manner.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: How much weight is placed on success and victories in tournaments and competitions?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: To be clear, Sir, I am not saying that sporting success is the only or most important measure in determining if an NSA is performing well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Rather, I believe that it is also in the public interest that senior appointments in NSAs are also carried out in a way that ensures that the best available person for the job is hired, especially since public monies are involved.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Chairman, as much as it pains me to say this, the fact that Singapore has not been doing well recently on the international football scene is an understatement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: While Singapore has clearly had success in the past, winning the AFF Suzuki Cup in 2012, the team's performance in recent editions and in other tournaments has, indeed, been below par.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: There has not been much success in finding a good head coach either, with the new coach joining in January after his predecessor lasted, I believe, less than two years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the area of high-performance sports, can MCCY share its plans to encourage more Singaporeans to donate to the One Team Singapore Fund?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can MCCY also share the plans to support Team Singapore athletes in preparing for the upcoming major games?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In community sports, sports in our everyday lives, can MCCY provide an update on its plan to upgrade existing sports facilities and build new ones to encourage sports participation?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Lastly, in terms of making sports a part of our lifestyle, can MCCY share if there are plans to bring in more major sporting events to add vibrancy to our sports scene?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we must go beyond physical accessibility to ensure that PwDs feel welcomed, supported and empowered to participate in sports activities alongside their peers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, could MCCY expand the range of sports programmes offered to cater to more disabilities?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Based on my survey, it also seems that not many PwDs have taken part in a SportSG or Para Sport Academy programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond partnering disability organisations, I encourage MCCY to consider ramping up its efforts on increasing outreach of its programmes to motivate more PwDs to take part.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Recalling the pandemic, many of us felt a sense of loss when safe management measures put a pause on many arts, exercise, sports and outdoor activities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some, like our seniors, missed the joy of learning; while others, like our youths, longed for the happiness from camaraderie of common pursuit.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The joy and happiness that enhanced our health and well-being were made possible by a community of dedicated coaches and instructors, who I shall refer to as "coaches".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The pandemic struck hard at coaches' livelihood and self-worth.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, some have gotten back on track while others have chosen to leave coaching.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In today's uncertain world, arts, exercise, sports and outdoor remain essential to strengthening and uniting Singaporeans across ages.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We must thus support coaches to keep faith.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As micro-businesses, they are expected to thrive regardless of the pressures from big service buyers and price competition and the struggles from shouldering interlocking business, personal and family responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: MCCY and its relevant agencies – the National Arts Council, Sports Singapore and People's Association – guide the professional development of arts, exercise, sports and outdoor Coaches.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, MCCY and its agencies have dedicated much effort and resources to uplifting coaching and instructing standards.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Initiatives, such as the National Registry of Exercise Professionals and Competency Framework for Arts Educators, are noteworthy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: NICA members and their fellow Coaches appreciate the Government's affirmation of their support and of their contribution and impact.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like other workers, they ask if the affirmation could translate to professional recognition and wage growth.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many coaches have told NICA that they struggle to adjust their fees to factor in the rising costs of operations, such as venue booking, and essentials ,such as meals, insurances and healthcare.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is because corporate and Government buyers often resist adjusting budgets for services on the one hand; even though on the other hand, they feel obliged to raise wages for their own staff because of rising costs of living.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because freelance coaches are microservice providers that are up against big and dominant service buyers, they often feel compelled to meet buyers' price expectations even when rates are on the downside and unsustainable in the long run.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I would like to propose three possibilities for the Minister's consideration.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The guidance would articulate the survey costs of coaches as freelancers delivering professional instruction to different segments of Singaporeans, especially as Healthier SG comes on stream.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The guidance could consider how similar qualified professions are remunerated and suggest differentiated premiums for coaches who upskill and attain different levels of mastery.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Most important, the guidance assures buyers of transparency and coaches of structured recognition for their contribution.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Not-for-profit entities could be tapped to manage the bookings.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so would allow talents in different fields to flourish and also nourish the entrepreneurial spirit in Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, the Sports Facilities Master Plan could allow sports and exercise coaches to directly tap repurposed spaces, such as refurbished schools.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These coaches could in turn cater classes for more Singaporeans at dedicated and convenient venues.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Against the backdrop of Healthier SG, NICA is putting together upskilling pathways to equip our members to coach niche segments, such as persons with disabilities and frail seniors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We are also familiarising coaches with AI and other emerging knowledge that can help to sharpen their edge.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: NICA welcomes more hands on deck to advance efforts.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By unlocking these three possibilities, we can support our freelance coaches for arts, exercise sports and outdoor adventure education to make a fair living, access opportunities on a level playing field; and like fellow Singaporeans, be equipped to take forward prospects on the horizon.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Let us empower those who help us to live life happy, healthy and well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Usha Chandradas, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This appears to be a relatively small amount as compared to the overall $100 million which has been committed to the rollout of the latest Arts Plan.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I may be misreading the numbers and if I am, I am very happy to stand corrected, but is the Ministry able to clarify how the $100 million of allocated funds will be applied over each of the four years, including the upcoming financial year?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry also be able to explain the rationale behind the allocation of these yearly amounts of expenditure?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The availability of art spaces, for example, is a perennial hot topic.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Ministry be working with MND to ensure that the unique artistic character of Gillman Barracks will be preserved or will the space be completely transformed?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If it is to be the latter, will alternative spaces be then set aside for the present tenants of Gillman Barracks?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, my second cut relates to the spending allocated for the building of the Cultural Concierge in FY2024.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I also have some questions on the expenditure, which has been planned for the Culture Sector Data Analytics Solution.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This has been budgeted at around $1.7 million.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With regard to the Cultural Concierge, I would like to declare my interest here as the owner of a local digital art magazine.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Ministry able to clarify what the expenditure relating to the Cultural Concierge will entail?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Ministry is aware, there are a number of independent digital content creators in the industry who all work with the aim of promoting awareness of the arts and in publicising arts events.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some platforms are more lucrative than others, some are purely run as passion projects; but what all creators in the space have in common is their commitment and passion in promoting awareness of the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They have put in resources to this end and some have spent years on their work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In developing its new digital platforms, what opportunities are there for the Ministry to work with existing independent content creators in the arts space?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: How can the public and private sectors work together in this area to improve arts appreciation, consumption and awareness amongst general audiences?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On the spending that is planned for the Cultural Sector Data Analytics Solution, can the Ministry provide details on what the expenditure will entail and what effect it is intended to have?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that while audience preferences are catered for in arts offerings, that there is still room for the avant-garde and works and events that push boundaries?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These two play an important long-term role in challenging and educating audiences on arts and cultural appreciation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This was a point that I made as well in my adjournment Motion last year.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that while our arts offerings are able to cater to popular demand, that there is still room for experimental and fringe activities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I certainly hope that the Government will continue to support these.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, for my third cut, I would like to ask the Ministry if it will consider converting Singapore's Cultural Medallion Award into a cash grant or cash award with incentives, such as health benefits.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This would be similar to national artistic awards given by our neighbours, such as Thailand and Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, to be clear, it is not a cash award.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is an entitlement to apply for funding for certain types of projects.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, these include projects that involve the mentoring of younger artists, the transfer of knowledge, community outreach and the development of the artist's own practice.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But there is an administrative application that has to be made and the funds are granted only if the application is approved.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question that I filed earlier this year, the Ministry clarified that 71% of living Cultural Medallion recipients have partially or fully used their access to this funding.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Of the recipients who had passed away and were eligible for the funding, 59% had partially or fully-utilised their entitlements.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For our national athletes who win medals internationally, cash awards are granted under the Major Games Award Programme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While these award amounts vary and athletes are required to plough back a certain percentage of the awards into their respective national sports associations, it is still a cash award and one which recognises the huge costs of training at an elite level.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It also serves as a reward for our athletes who play a big role in bringing Singaporeans together whenever they win medals.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Artists too, when they are at a developmental stage of their careers, incur significant costs in maintaining and growing their artistic practices.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As acknowledged by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in his Budget Statement, the arts play such an important role in making Singapore a distinctive home for us all.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Cultural Medallion is Singapore's highest arts accolade.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It would also provide them with a measure of monetary support in recognition of the financial sacrifices that are often required to build a career in the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in his announcement on the proposed new artist space at Kampong Java, Minister Edwin Tong said that the Government was prepared to let the arts community take the lead in telling the Government what they want.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He said, "A little bit of messiness in that space is something that I think we need." I fully agree with this sentiment and I know that many in the arts community do as well and I thank the Minister for this affirmation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry be able to provide details on how these big picture ideas will be operationalised, both in 45 Arminian Street and in the new art spaces that will be coming up in this year?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore is a multi-racial, multi-cultural country and there are several neighbourhoods that are representative of this and take pride in their unique identities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: These neighbourhoods have escaped the wrecking ball through careful planning, rebuilding and restoration and new life has indeed been injected in them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: One of these is Tiong Bahru, Singapore's oldest residential neighbourhood and is well known for its well-conserved art-deco architecture.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Now the place is alive with hipster cafes, boutiques and a vibrant community for all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Kampong Glam is a historic Malay/Muslim neighbourhood featuring the iconic architectural and cultural features such as the Sultan Mosque, Arab Street and the Malay Heritage Centre, a reflection of traditional Malay architecture indeed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Chinatown is a bustling neighbourhood, rich with Chinese culture and heritage.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Here we see traditional pre-war shophouses, together with street markets and cultural attractions such as the Thian Hock Keng Temple.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Of course, Little India is another showcase of Singapore's Indian heritage and culture.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This is home to the beautiful and bustling temples in Little India which date back to the 19th century.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Besides the temples, Little India is dotted with colourful streets and Indian eateries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: And, of course, Joo Chiat and Katong are unmistakably Peranakan neighbourhoods that are filled with colourful shophouses, wonderful cuisine and cultural landmarks such as the Katong Antique House.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: And this rich history and legacy is manifested in a unique tapestry of places and is a placeholder for us to grow together even as we are anchored in this heritage and culture of the past.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As we continue to welcome people from all over the world, our cultural heritage will grow to take a confident hold of the future while harkening back to the past – our roots.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Can MCCY share how we will create opportunities to enliven these and other neighbourhoods, celebrate their rich heritage and foster a stronger sense of belonging and identity?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Initiatives over the years have included the establishment of community arts and culture clubs across different neighbourhoods in Singapore to offer a variety of arts and cultural activities for residents to participate in.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Another initiative is a strong emphasis on arts education in school, ensuring that students have exposure to various forms of arts and cultural expressions from young.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Art education is premised on openness and diversity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: NAC's Art Education Unit, I believe, works closely with the arts community and various agencies, including the Ministry of Education (MOE), the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) and the Preschool Anchor Operators (AOPs) to provide an access to a range of well-designed arts education experiences with Singapore artists and arts groups.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Indeed, the arts can help foster connectedness, inclusivity and collaboration, strengthening social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: In this regard, can MCCY provide an update on the efforts to ensure diverse art spaces that serve as touchpoints for both the public and artists?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important for us to age healthily to reduce the growing burden on our healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Amongst the various measures implemented by the Government, an effective one is using arts to promote and enhance health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The arts has a role to play in preventing, managing and treating physical and mental disorders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Music and dance can help motor rehabilitation after a stroke.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singing in a choir, making art or group drumming can ease anxiety and depression." Would the Minister provide an update on broad-based mental well-being support in the arts and its role in Healthier SG?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MCCY share more about the specific art-based programmes and resources that promote health and well-being?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, festivals, programmes and resources that arts groups can use for selected target segments such as the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are the initiatives to support and promote the wellbeing of art practitioners, including freelancers?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Chairman, in our rapidly evolving societal landscape, the role of the arts in promoting citizens' health and well-being has become increasingly significant.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: As Singapore grapples with the challenges posed by an ageing population, there arises a pressing need for innovative interventions to enhance the quality of life and overall well-being of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I am keen to understand the strategies MCCY has in place in utilising our heritage assets, notably museums to foster community bonding, national pride and unity under the Forward SG movement.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How are these cultural assets planned to be leveraged for cultural exchange, celebrating our heritage and building a resilient national identity?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry provide insights on increasing museum accessibility, digital engagement and educational outreach such that the public understands their contribution towards a cohesive and future-ready Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Chairman, one of Singapore's fundamental tenets of our social compact is to strive towards being a multiracial, multi-cultural and multi-religious community, living harmoniously together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I say "strive", because this element of our social compact is something we need to constantly keep in our minds and work towards improving.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Because no matter how well we think we are on this call, it is not something that can be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We need only look at the conflicts around the world to understand that racial, cultural and religious differences can often lead to unimaginable hardship and suffering for communities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The preservation of our diverse cultural heritage is an important way for us to foster a strong sense of belonging and a shared identity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We have neighbourhoods such as Geylang Serai, Little India and Chinatown that are culture-rich and many Singaporeans take pride in their unique identity and culture.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: More can be done to create opportunities to celebrate these culture-rich places.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Further, we should take the opportunity to empower our youths in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Our youths represent the next generation of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Through the Forward SG exercise, they have expressed their desire to play an active role in shaping policies and co-creating the communities they live in.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, as mentioned by the Member just before me, we have a rich heritage.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our ability to forge racial and religious mutual respect today stems from our decades of living together, working together and facing challenges together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It was not The changing world will require us to deepen our unique heritage and stay united as one people, stemming from our different races, our different cultures and our different religious affiliations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Engaging our youths in appreciating and preserving our cultural and societal heritage needs to continue.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It was encouraging to see higher visitor numbers to our museums and heritage institutions in the recent years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, as a multiracial country, social harmony is key to ensuring that our community stays together as one people, one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Yet, issues exist, and we are witnessing conflicts around the world with ethnic and religious angles and undertones that could have a possible adverse effect on our society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Several conflicts around the world have indeed taken on ethnic dimensions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The impact of the Gaza crisis has affected communities on both sides of the conflict that started on 7 October 2023.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The Russian-Ukraine war is also an ethnic one, largely involving ethnic Russians and Ukrainians.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The annexation of Crimea by Russia and the ongoing war in Donetsk and Luhansk since early 2022 have only heightened ethnic, linguistic and cultural divisions in the region.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Sadly, neither one of these two conflicts look like they will end any time soon.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Another long-drawn conflict in Syria is a clash of ethnic groups such as the Turkmen, Kurds, Arabs and Assyrians, among others.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: We have also seen civil war in South Sudan between the Dinka and Nuer ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The Boko Haram insurgency in Nigeria is another example of a conflict with ethnic and religious undertones.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: These are just a few examples and many other regions around the world experience conflict with ethnic and religious dimensions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Understanding and resolving these conflicts often require addressing deep-seated historical grievances, promoting inclusive governance and fostering inter-ethnic dialogue and reconciliation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Despite our diversity, we have managed to build and maintain a strong and united society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This can aptly be described as an unusual modus vivendi.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Amidst this, there are incidents that arise from time to time that threaten our balance and some incidents may result in a lingering sentiment, especially amongst our minority groups.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Migrants may also pose challenges to our unity as they go through the process of integrating into our way of life.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Maintaining our racial and religious harmony is therefore an ongoing effort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is not a natural balance and significant effort must continuously be expended by the Government to steward our social harmony together with other stakeholders like community groups and religious organisations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister update on MCCY's efforts to bolster our racial and religious harmony and its priorities in the coming year?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Hany Soh, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, our youths are a key and valuable segment of our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their views, feedback and ideas must be heard, not least because they often inject fresh perspectives and introduce new dimensions to thought processes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask how has MCCY been encouraging and supporting our youths to experiment and transform their ideas into tangible actions and to fruition?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How else and how better can MCCY provide their encouragement and support?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As it approaches its five-year mark, are there any updates that MCCY can share on the outcomes achieved and the number of projects implemented from the Challenge thus far?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mental well-being continues to be an important issue in the minds of Singaporeans, particularly our youths.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can MCCY provide an update on the Network's progress in meeting its objective and, specifically, the assessed effectiveness of the Well-Being Circles in supporting mental health and mental well-being?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can these initiatives rolled out by MCCY synergise with other ground-up initiatives introduced by local divisions?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Take, for example, in our Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC's Woodgrove division, we recognise that it is crucial to raise awareness of the importance of mental health and well-being and establish a strong community support network to encourage those who are in need to seek help.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This year, a series of mental wellness-related workshops has been planned to take place in Woodgrove, from training our grassroots leaders with skills, such as active listening and psychological first aid to equipping families with better awareness on youths and seniors-related mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, last weekend, Jurong GRC and M³@Jurong organised a flash mentoring programme for students who had just received their "A" level results.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We collaborated with MENDAKI and SINDA which recommended some of their accomplished volunteers to be mentors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some were students from law school or awaiting entry into Cambridge; some were young professionals but all so eager to share their insights with our youths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The programme, known as School of Day 1, was coordinated by Mohammad Matin Mohdari.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Matin and the mentors worked hard to curate a meaningful session where difficult topics were broken down to actionable steps.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am certain the participants took away very useful learning points.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there are also efforts to build the capability of mentors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What has been the outcome of all the efforts thus far?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, how successful has Mentoring SG been in providing mentoring opportunities to the youths?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also feel that it is important to work with people and organisations in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Has there been meaningful collaboration with the stakeholders in the community and corporate partners in this endeavour?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: A quick look at our history will show accounts of individuals from all races generously giving back over the centuries.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Many familiar names can be found in hospital and healthcare facilities, educational institutions, community services.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Many contributions are captured in our archives: individuals and families from all walks of life giving time, talents and treasures.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: As we shape our new social compact, there are many ways we can continue to engage all of society across all ages and at all levels.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Developing the Company of Good will bring about giving from our extensive business community.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, there are many ways that corporations can support the vulnerable and those in need.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Offering their professional resources and expertise is one way.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Can MCCY share how it will work with the ESG Coordination Office to support businesses in integrating social impact into their business models, and what is the progress thus far?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC) also has its Company of Good programme to encourage businesses to do good.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Can MCCY share how can the ESG Coordination Office and NVPC better synergise efforts and also share its plans to encourage the business community and working professionals to contribute more to society beyond just making corporate donations and volunteering?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Chairman, since 1925, co-operative societies (co-ops) have been playing a pivotal role in Singapore, alongside the Government and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that the business model of co-ops serve the people's social and economic needs in bad times and not just in good times.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: For example, NTUC FairPrice ensured that daily essentials remained available and affordable, and the FairPrice on Wheels service was launched to bring essential groceries within walking distance of homes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: I am heartened that the Government has engaged the co-op community as part of the Forward SG dialogue.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: As such, how can co-ops be further supported to continue their unique role alongside other business entities in the "Do Good" space, thereby reinforcing Singapore's commitment to social cohesion and inclusive growth?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Chairman, there are many grassroots leaders in Bukit Batok East who are seniors and I am often inspired and heartened by their energy and commitment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One of them is Judy Leong, an 82-year-old lady who has been a volunteer for about 35 years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Judy lives alone as her husband had passed away some years ago and she does not have any children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But Judy's life is full, as she spends her days engaging with residents and helping out at various community events.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I want to be like Judy when I am older.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are all cognisant of the issues relating to ageing in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We know that mental and social well-being are important and that we need to actively engage seniors so they are not socially isolated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One meaningful way to do so is to encourage volunteerism.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I note that there have been efforts in place like partnerships with organisations like RSVP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In some spaces, we are also seeing an increase in the number of senior volunteers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While there are positive news, we should continue to build a culture such that people want to volunteer after they have retired or when they reach their silver years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We should have a deeper understanding of the current demography.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, we are looking at younger seniors who are more educated or tech-savvy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Look at what opportunities interest them and put in place a more structured approach to create more avenues of participation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I hope to hear the Ministry's plans on encouraging senior volunteerism.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you like, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can MCCY share the impact VCs have had in building a culture of care and how this impact will be sustained?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What have been the challenges and experiences gained over the years?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I know there have been some changes of operators in some towns.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What are the reasons for these changes and how has MCCY been managing the disruption?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The needs in each town are varied and span across a spectrum.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Besides social service agencies and charities, there are Government agencies, such as Silver Generation Office, requiring volunteers, too.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: At the same time, while there could be some town-specific demographic characteristics that require VCs to have different focus areas and strategies, there will be some commonalities as the Singapore population is generally ageing and the importance of mental health applies across all age groups.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can MCCY share how it will strengthen the VCs' capabilities to attract, engage and sustain volunteers more effectively in meeting the diverse needs?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How do the VCs cross-share and cross-learn from one another?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is expected that many volunteers are retirees or people who do not work full time as they would have more time to spare.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, there are specific skills and networks that working professionals can bring to the table.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How have the VCs been able to reach out to this group of potential volunteers?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In each town, there will also be businesses and corporates, both big and small, where their staff could be encouraged to volunteer, too.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can MCCY share its plans in encouraging corporates to join the SG Cares movement?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can MCCY share how SGPO will drive Government-citizen partnerships?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The Partners Portal has a useful listing of all partnership receptacles, grants and volunteering networks available in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I think this is a good starting point as citizens can sometimes be confused and do not know the existing resources available.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Getting help in navigating to the right agency and contacts can accelerate the process and help to put good intentions to actions quickly.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: A proposal may not receive funding from more than one Government grant or scheme.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Can MCCY share how citizens will be supported to materialise their proposals, especially those that may fall between the cracks?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: As all new initiatives will have some teething issues, I wish SGPO all the very best in its journey to forge a closer partnership between citizens and the Government.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have now come to the end of the cuts for MCCY.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the last few days we have discussed and debated many serious policy announcements in this House: from tackling immediate cost of living issues and concerns; creating good jobs for Singaporeans; reshaping our economy; to meeting housing demands; reimagining the future of education; and our response to climate change, to name a few.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many of these are policies which strike at the heart of Singapore's long-term interests.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And these are very important matters for Singapore and Singaporeans, and some are even existential ones.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But equally important is for us to achieve them together: as one people, united in our cause with a collective vision and a shared aspiration for Singapore's future.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is the spirit of Forward Singapore (Forward SG), led by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Which brings to my mind an old African proverb: if you want to go fast, go alone; but if you want to go far, go together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our unity has been our strength behind every success in our history.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Few societies in the world have succeeded in societal harmony, let alone one that is as richly diverse as ours.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In today's increasingly divided world, fraught with war, rising inequality, misinformation, populist movements, political disenchantment, this unity is all the more rare and precious.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is ours to cherish and protect if Singapore is to succeed in our next chapter.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is why it is fitting that the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) brings up the end of the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our work is diverse: from developing the arts and sports; stewarding our treasured heritage; empowering our youths; corporates and community; to give back; care for others; and come together to build Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the heart of everything we do is our goal to foster unity, cohesion and that unique Singaporean identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This underscores all that we do at MCCY.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And it is the powerful unifying force that helps us transcend our differences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have seen this come to life when we rallied behind our national heroes in sports and in the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Syed Harun yesterday made a very impassioned speech, noting that when Joseph Schooling won his Olympic gold medal, or when Loh Kean Yew became world champion, or when Shanti took on the very best in Asia and beat them all, we all remember and cherish those moments, we feel proud of their sporting achievements; but even prouder because each of these athletes represents something in each of us and, collectively, as Singaporeans, and it ignites our shared Singapore spirit.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the same way, our history is brightly lit with the many cultural icons who have inspired and united us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Iskandar Jalil is a master at pottery, but he also creates poetry with his hands.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The late Santha Bhaskar, who exemplified a deep appreciation for diversity, embodied multiculturalism throughout her life's work.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond sporting and artistic successes, though, these stories also teach us about strength, resilience, creativity and excellence; inspiring present and future generations to dream big in a pursuit of excellence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is why even in difficult times, it is so important that we continue to cultivate and nurture and develop our sportsmen and our artists.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, Sir, in my response, I will set out the broad overarching framework of MCCY's efforts in these areas.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My colleagues will develop the details further in their speeches – Minister of State Low Yen Ling on the arts; Minister of State Alvin Tan on the giving space as well as our youths; and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua on sports.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our most basic goal is to drive interest and participation in sports.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are obvious strong social benefits, from keeping active and fit to encouraging intermixing and through that, strengthening our bonds and our social cohesion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is also the basic building block to finding that next wave of high-performing athletes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A broader base leads to a stronger and more sustained pipeline for talent.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singaporeans are already getting more active in sporting.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, through accessible sport programmes in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our young can, today, join sports co-curricular activities (CCAs).

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can also take part in junior sports academy programmes in primary schools, ActiveSG programmes or even take part in private academies and clubs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will recall that last year we topped-up the ActiveSG credits, so that these credits can be used to defray the cost of courses run by ActiveSG at any of their programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even if young people do not come from well-to-do backgrounds, SportCares is a programme that is set up to enable children from low-income families to also be included.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Other programmes, like the Saturday Night Lights football programme, helps to equip youths with holistic life skills using sport, in this case, football as a medium.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the grassroots level, Singaporeans from all walks of life can take part in exciting community-level competitions and games.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, I am very pleased to announce that this year, People's Association (PA), working with SportSG, will bring back the popular inter-constituency as well as inter-GRC community championship as part of Pesta Sukan, which means Festival of Sport.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Teams will compete under the banner of their constituency, with a final round amongst the GRCs to determine the national champion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will no doubt add some competitive spirit in community games.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we have been working on having more sporting facilities close to where Singaporeans live.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In many Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates, there are now free-to-play facilities like basketball or futsal courts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some of them are fenced up so that you can protect passersby from a stray ball.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In many of them, there are also badminton or sepak takraw courts, which sometimes also doubles up as pickleball courts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, we are also building up an island-wide network of world-class sporting facilities right in your neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One example is the Toa Payoh Integrated Development in the heart of a mature town.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This new development will have top-notch sporting facilities to cater to a range of activities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will benefit not only the athletes who train there, but also heartlanders, both young and old, who come together, play and bond through sport.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are many more other developments coming soon at the heartlands in Punggol, Clementi, Queenstown, Ang Mo Kio and Hougang.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, we recognise that Singaporeans are interested in a broader range of diverse sports, some of which might not yet have mainstream appeal.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will catalyse even more support for our national athletes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman and Mr Darryl David spoke about this and they will be pleased to know that with OTSF, we will do more for emerging sports that are gaining traction in the community and where our athletes also do well on the international stage.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These additional resources will also mean that these sports can encourage more grassroots participation and broaden the base, as I noted earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric will speak more about the expansion of OTSF to include SportCares.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as we talk about growing the base of participation, we also want to ensure that persons with disabilities (PwDs), are included.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also on track to make all ActiveSG gyms inclusive by 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Having the hardware and the physical set-up to accommodate PwDs is a good step forward, but we cannot just be satisfied that a PwD can navigate the pool and gyms with barrier-free access and then think that, that is enough and stop there.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have to go further and support them with inclusive programming to build a community and to also have appropriately trained coaches to run these programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, when you visit our facilities, you can tap into a range of disability sport and inclusive sport programmes and services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, more than 3,000 individuals have attended disability awareness training and various coaching and technical courses to better support the PwDs' participation in sport, to allow them to take part actively in the programmes.
